portName: Port of Casablanca (Casablanca Cruise Port, Jetée Moulay Youssef)
townName: the Old Medina and city centre
seoTitle: Casablanca cruise port guide: mosque, medina and trains
seoDescription: New 2025 terminal about 1 km from the centre. Hassan II Mosque tours 140 MAD (2026); taxis are unmetered, agree the fare. Back on board 60 min early.
quickAnswer: Ships berth alongside at the new cruise terminal on the Jetée Moulay Youssef, opened in September 2025 inside the working port, about 1 km from the city centre. Walking out through the port is not recommended; use the port shuttle or a taxi, agreeing the fare first (about €10 to the centre in 2026). Be back on board 60 minutes before all-aboard; on a Rabat trip, be on a train into Casa Port 2 hours before.
intro: Casablanca is Morocco's commercial capital, not a postcard town, and the cruise day works best with a clear plan. The one sight everyone comes for is the Hassan II Mosque on the ocean, which non-Muslims can enter only on timed guided tours. Around it sit the walled Old Medina next to the port, the 1930s Habous quarter, the art deco centre and the Corniche. Marrakech is about 240 km away and Rabat about 90 km, so a day trip to either one depends on trains or a long coach ride. Traffic is heavy on weekdays, so allow more time for the return than the map suggests.

terminals.name: Casablanca Cruise Terminal (Jetée Moulay Youssef)
terminals.notes: Inaugurated on 18 September 2025; first ship 26 September 2025. About 650 m of quay, three gangways (one fixed, two telescopic), a terminal building and parking for 44 coaches. Takes ships up to 350 m long. Operated by Global Ports Holding under a 15-year concession from 1 January 2026. One guide notes that shops and amenities are still limited.

walkability.detail: The city centre is about 1–1.25 km from the berth, but the route crosses a working industrial port and depends on which passenger exit is open. Guides advise against walking it, especially in heat. Once in town the Old Medina is walkable; the mosque, the Habous quarter and the Corniche need a taxi.

transportSections.mode: Port or cruise line shuttle bus
transportSections.cost: Free or a small charge, depending on the line (2026)
transportSections.time: Short ride to the city centre
transportSections.detail: Shuttles run from the terminal to the centre; United Nations Square near the Old Medina is a common stop. Check the drop-off point and the last return time in your daily programme.

transportSections.cost: About €10 to the centre; the return is often cheaper (2026)
transportSections.time: Short ride to the centre; slower in weekday traffic
transportSections.detail: Taxis wait at the dockside. Port taxis do not run on meters, so agree the destination and the fare before you get in. Carry small dirham notes.

transportSections.mode: Train to Rabat (from Casa Port station)
transportSections.cost: About US$4 second class, US$8 first class one way (2026 guide estimate)
transportSections.time: About 75 minutes to Rabat Ville; roughly hourly
transportSections.detail: Casa Port station is about 20 minutes' walk or a short taxi ride from the port. Al Boraq high-speed trains from Casa Voyageurs reach Rabat Agdal in about 30 minutes. Buy tickets at the station; cards are accepted.

transportSections.cost: From about US$21 one way; first class about US$25–32 (2026 booking site)
transportSections.time: About 2 h 40 min to just over 4 hours each way
transportSections.detail: Classic Al Atlas trains. With 5–8 hours of rail travel in a day this is not a sensible independent trip on a normal port call; take the ship's excursion if you want Marrakech.
Useful only once you are in town, for example along the Corniche. A taxi is simpler for most cruise visitors.

returnTiming.rule: Be back on board 60 minutes before all-aboard if you stayed in Casablanca; on a Rabat trip, be on a train due into Casa Port at least 2 hours before all-aboard.
returnTiming.detail: Weekday rush-hour traffic is slow, and the drive from the Corniche or the Habous quarter to the port can take much longer than the distance suggests. Taxis have to reach the terminal through the port gates. Leave the city 30 minutes earlier than you think you need to: from the centre, the mosque, the Habous quarter or the Corniche, set off for the port at least 105 minutes before all-aboard.
returnTiming.emergencyFallback: Take a taxi straight to the cruise terminal and show the driver the port name in your daily programme. If you will miss all-aboard, call the port agent number printed on your daily programme.

diyVsExcursion.item: Hassan II Mosque and city sights
diyVsExcursion.ship: Varies by line; check your cruise planner
Varies by line; check your cruise planner
diyVsExcursion.diy: Train from about US$21 each way, 2 h 40 min to 4 h each way (2026)

excursionAdvice: Skip the ship tour for Casablanca itself if you are comfortable negotiating taxis: the mosque runs fixed-time tours you can join on your own, and the medina and Habous quarter are short rides apart. Take the ship's excursion for Marrakech. It is about 240 km away, the train alone takes close to three hours or more each way, and if a train runs late the ship will not wait. Rabat is the borderline case: fine by train on a long call if you build in a large margin, easier on a ship tour.

dayPlan.intro: Assumes the ship docks at 08:00 and all-aboard is 17:30, outside Ramadan, on a day other than Friday.

steps.what: Off the ship. Take the shuttle or agree a taxi fare at the quay for the Hassan II Mosque.
Arrive at the mosque in clothes that cover shoulders and knees. Buy tickets (140 MAD) for the 10:00 tour, or the 09:00 tour if you are early.
Guided tour of the prayer hall. Shoes are removed and carried in a bag.
Walk along the ocean front, then into the Old Medina for its lanes and walls.
Lunch at La Sqala, the restored 18th-century bastion on the medina walls.
Taxi to the Habous quarter for its arcaded souks and pastries at Pâtisserie Bennis.
Taxi to Mohammed V Square and the art deco centre; short stop only.
Taxi or shuttle back to the cruise terminal, allowing for traffic.
Back on board, 60 minutes before all-aboard.

sights.name: Hassan II Mosque
sights.why: Morocco's largest mosque, beside the Atlantic, with one of the world's tallest minarets. One of the few mosques in Morocco open to non-Muslims, on guided tours.
sights.cost: 140 MAD foreign adult; 30 MAD children over 6; under 6 free (2026)
sights.tip: Tours at 09:00, 10:00, 11:00 and 12:00 plus 15:00 (and 16:00 from mid-March to mid-September). On Fridays only 09:00 and 10:00 run in the morning, and the Ramadan timetable is different. Cover shoulders and knees; shorts and sleeveless tops are refused.

sights.name: Old Medina
sights.why: The walled old town beside the port: narrow lanes, small markets and everyday city life.
sights.tip: Use an offline map, as the lanes are confusing. Decline offers from unofficial guides.

sights.name: La Sqala
sights.why: An 18th-century bastion on the medina walls, restored around 2001 and now a garden restaurant.
sights.cost: Free to look; meal prices not verified
sights.tip: Book for lunch; breakfast can be walk-in.

sights.name: Quartier Habous
sights.why: A 'new medina' built by the French in the 1930s, with arcaded craft souks, bookshops and pastry shops.
sights.tip: About 5 km from the waterfront; take a taxi and agree the fare.

sights.name: Mohammed V Square and the art deco centre
sights.why: The civic heart of the French-era city, with the modern Grand Theatre and many 1920s–30s buildings.
sights.tip: Casamémoire, a local heritage group, runs donation-based architecture walks; arrange in advance.

sights.name: Sacré-Cœur Cathedral
sights.why: A deconsecrated 1930s church, earmarked to become a cultural centre.
sights.tip: Opening for events varies; treat it as an exterior stop.

sights.name: Rick's Café
sights.why: A restaurant built to recreate the bar from the film Casablanca, near the medina walls.
sights.tip: Book ahead and note there is a dress code. The live jazz starts at 21:30, after most ships sail.

sights.name: Rabat (day trip)
sights.why: Morocco's capital, about 90 km north, reachable by train.
sights.cost: Train about US$4–8 each way (2026 guide estimate) plus taxis
sights.tip: Only on a long call. Aim to be back at Casa Port at least 2 hours before all-aboard.

beaches.name: Corniche (Aïn Diab)
beaches.time: About 8–10 km from the terminal by taxi; journey time depends heavily on traffic
beaches.note: A long ocean promenade with beach clubs and cafés. Atlantic surf and currents are strong, and many Moroccan beaches have little or no lifeguard cover.

food.dish: Traditional Moroccan breakfast: eggs with khlii (preserved dried meat), msemen, baghrir

food.where: Central Market (Marché Central), city centre: buy fish and have a nearby café grill it

food.dish: Mint tea and coffee in an old-style café

commonMistakes.mistake: Arriving at the mosque in shorts or a sleeveless top.
commonMistakes.fix: Cover shoulders, torso and knees. The rules forbid shorts and sleeveless clothes.

commonMistakes.mistake: Turning up at the mosque between tour times, or for a midday tour on a Friday.
commonMistakes.fix: Check the tour times before leaving the ship. On Fridays the last morning tour is 10:00.

commonMistakes.mistake: Getting into a taxi without agreeing the fare.
commonMistakes.fix: Agree the destination and price before setting off, and carry small dirham notes.

commonMistakes.mistake: Trying to do Marrakech independently by train.
commonMistakes.fix: It is close to three hours or more each way by train. Use the ship's excursion.

commonMistakes.mistake: Walking out of the port from the ship.
commonMistakes.fix: Use the shuttle or a taxi; the route goes through a working port and the exit points vary.

commonMistakes.mistake: Planning on cash machines or changing money back at the end.
commonMistakes.fix: Dirhams cannot be taken out of Morocco or easily changed back. Withdraw only what you need and spend it.

safety: Casablanca is a large, busy city. Petty theft is common in medinas and crowded areas: pickpocketing, bag-snatching and thefts of visible jewellery and bags by passing motorcyclists. Keep valuables out of sight and avoid quiet streets. Traffic is fast and road crossings need care. The UK government notes that people posing as official guides often harass tourists; official guides carry a badge. Women may receive unwanted attention; loose clothing that covers arms and legs helps, and it is required for the mosque anyway. Do not swim off isolated beaches: the Atlantic surf is strong and lifeguards are often absent.
scams: Unofficial guides in and around the medina who attach themselves to visitors and then demand payment. Official guides carry a badge; decline politely and keep walking.
Taxi fares that change at the end of the ride. Agree the price before getting in or insist on the meter.
Strangers offering directions who lead you to a shop or ask for money. Use an offline map.
Card fraud and goods swapped for inferior ones after purchase. Watch your card and check items before they are wrapped.
accessibility: The berth is alongside with gangways, so there is no tender transfer. The mosque's huge courtyard and prayer hall are level, but shoes must be removed and carried. The Old Medina has narrow, uneven lanes and is hard going for wheelchairs; the Corniche promenade and the centre around Mohammed V Square are flatter and wider. Ask the ship whether its shuttle buses are accessible, and arrange an accessible car through the shore excursion desk if needed, as ordinary taxis are small.
rainyDay: The mosque tour is mostly indoors and works in any weather. Add the covered souks of the Habous quarter, a long lunch at a restaurant, and the Museum of Moroccan Judaism (closed Saturdays). Skip the Corniche walk in rain and wind.
crowdTips: The mosque is the bottleneck: ship tours and independent visitors aim for the same tour slots. Take the earliest tour you can reach, and avoid Friday midday, when there are no tours after 10:00. The medina and Habous quarter are calmest in the early afternoon. On weekdays leave the Corniche or Habous for the port before the late-afternoon rush.

faqs.a: No. Ships normally berth alongside at the cruise terminal on the Jetée Moulay Youssef.

faqs.q: Is Casablanca walkable from the cruise port?
faqs.a: Only partly. The centre is about 1 km away, but the route crosses a working port and is not recommended. Use the shuttle or a taxi to the mosque, then walk the medina.

faqs.q: How do I get from Casablanca cruise port to the Hassan II Mosque?
faqs.a: By taxi from the quay, agreeing the fare first, or by the port shuttle to the centre and a taxi from there.

faqs.q: How much is the Hassan II Mosque tour?
faqs.a: 140 MAD for foreign adults and 30 MAD for children over 6 in 2026. Tours run at fixed times, mostly 09:00 to 12:00 and 15:00, with fewer on Fridays.

faqs.q: Can I visit Marrakech from Casablanca cruise port?
faqs.a: Only realistically on the ship's excursion. Marrakech is about 240 km away and the train takes about 2 h 40 min to over 4 hours each way.

faqs.q: Can I visit Rabat from Casablanca on a cruise?
faqs.a: Yes on a long call. Trains from Casa Port take about 75 minutes to Rabat Ville. Be back at Casa Port at least 2 hours before all-aboard.

faqs.q: What can I do in Casablanca in one day from a cruise ship?
faqs.a: A morning mosque tour, the Old Medina and lunch at La Sqala, then the Habous quarter or the Corniche.

faqs.q: Is Casablanca safe for cruise passengers?
faqs.a: Generally, with big-city precautions. Watch for pickpockets and bag-snatchers, agree taxi fares and decline unofficial guides.
